---
title: "Are Black Friday Deals Real?"
subtitle: "Government price data says yes, prices really do dip in November. But the drop is small, and it doesn't come close to undoing this year's price increases."
author: "SixtyEight95"
date: "2026-11-27"
categories: [holidays, shopping, cost of living]
image: infographic.png
---

```{r setup}
source("../../R/fred.R")
source("../../R/black_friday_data.R")
library(knitr)
pct <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(ifelse(x > 0, "+", ""), formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
f1 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)
items <- bf_prices %>% filter(item %in% c("Clothing", "Toys", "Computers"))
```

Every year the signs say "50% OFF" and "LOWEST PRICE EVER." So we checked whether prices actually go down around Black
Friday. To do that, we used the government's own price tracker, the Consumer Price Index, which records what people
**really pay** across thousands of stores.

## The short answer

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Yes, the deals are real, but small.** On average, what people pay for **clothing** drops about
**`r f1(abs(items$nov_change[1]))`%** from October to November, **toys** about **`r f1(abs(items$nov_change[2]))`%**, and **computers** about
**`r f1(abs(items$nov_change[3]))`%**. That's nothing like 50% off. And prices for those same things are **up `r f1(items$yoy[1])`% to `r f1(items$yoy[3])`%**
from a year ago, so a Black Friday dip doesn't undo this year's price increases.
:::

## Prices really do dip in November

We looked at how prices changed from October to November and to December in every year from 2010 to 2024.

```{r drop table}
bf_prices %>%
  transmute(Item = item,
            `Oct → Nov (avg)` = pct(nov_change),
            `Oct → Dec (avg)` = pct(dec_change),
            `Years prices fell in Nov` = paste(years_fell, "of", years)) %>%
  kable(align = "lrrr", caption = "Source: BLS Consumer Price Index, not seasonally adjusted, 2010-2024.")
```

The dip is consistent. Clothing prices fell from October to November in **every one of those 15 years**. Toys and computers
fell in almost every year. Clothing keeps getting cheaper into December: by then it's about **`r f1(abs(items$dec_change[1]))`% below October**.

## So why isn't it 50% off?

A few reasons the signs and the data don't match:

- **Not everything is on sale.** The 50%-off doorbusters are a handful of items. The CPI tracks everything people buy.
- **"Original price" isn't always the usual price.** A discount off a list price that few people ever paid looks bigger
  than it really is.
- **Some categories get cheaper all year.** Toys and computers drift down over time as products improve, so part of
  their November drop would have happened anyway.

The takeaway: real deals exist, but the average shopper saves a few percent, not half.

## The catch: gifts cost more this year

```{r yoy table}
bf_prices %>%
  transmute(Item = item, `Price change, Sept 2025 → Sept 2026` = pct(yoy)) %>%
  kable(align = "lr", caption = "Source: BLS Consumer Price Index.")
```

Toys are up **`r f1(items$yoy[2])`%** and computers **`r f1(items$yoy[3])`%** from a year ago. A 1-2% November dip doesn't come close to
cancelling that out.

## We're spending more, but not buying more

The National Retail Federation expects holiday sales in November and December to reach **$`r nrf_2026_t` trillion**,
up **`r nrf_growth_2026`%** from last year. But overall prices are up **`r f1(cpi_yoy)`%**. After inflation, that's growth of only about
**`r f1(real_growth)`%**. In other words, we're paying more for roughly the same amount of stuff.

NRF's own survey found that **`r nrf_economy_share`%** of shoppers say the economy will affect their holiday spending.

## How to actually get a deal

- **Use a price tracker** (many browsers and sites have one) to see an item's real price history before you buy.
- **Clothing can wait.** The data says it gets cheaper into December.
- **Make a list and a budget.** The best deal is not buying something you didn't plan to.

## The fine print

- **CPI figures** are national averages of prices people actually paid, including sale prices. They are not seasonally
  adjusted, so they show the real November dip.
- **2025 is left out** of the October-to-November averages because the October 2025 CPI was never published, due to the
  government shutdown.
- **Year-over-year changes** compare September 2025 to September 2026, the latest month with data for both years.
- **The NRF forecast** excludes car dealers, gas stations, and restaurants.

---

**How we did this.** Prices are from the Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Price Index via FRED: apparel (CPIAPPNS), toys
(CUUR0000SERE01), computers (CUUR0000SEEE01), commodities less food (CUUR0000SACL1), and all items (CPIAUCNS). The holiday
forecast is from the National Retail Federation's October 15, 2026 release.
